title: The three-year retreat
hook: Kagyu and other schools keep retreats of three years and three fortnights

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kagyu: Tilopa, Naropa, Marpa and Milarepa, a teaching passed by mouth. Your line was the whispered lineage. What did you pass on, and to whom? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-one.

A door closes behind a small group of people in maroon robes. On the other side is a plain retreat house with a shrine room, a kitchen, narrow rooms, and a walled garden. Outside, friends and family wave. Inside, a bell rings before dawn, and a schedule begins that will run, day after day, through every season. Nobody inside will come out for a holiday or a wedding. When the door opens again, the people walking out will have spent three years and three fortnights at it. Today: the three-year retreat.
screen: `A DOOR CLOSES ON A RETREAT HOUSE.` → `A BELL BEFORE DAWN, EVERY DAY.` → `THE THREE-YEAR RETREAT.`

segments.voice: First, the length. Tradition sets the retreat at three years and three fortnights, a little more than three years. Kagyu teachers keep it, and so do other Tibetan schools. Different teachers give different reasons for the extra fortnights. What matters is that the time is fixed in advance and kept, not shortened when it gets hard. Second, what happens inside. The day runs from before dawn into the night in sessions of practice: prostrations, mantra, visualization, the teachings of the lineage, one after another, in the order a teacher lays out. Retreatants cook, clean, and keep silence for long stretches. Some Kagyu retreats include training in the practices that came down from Naropa. Third, why so long. The Kagyu school prizes practice over learning about practice. You met Naropa yesterday, putting down his books to find the meaning. You met Milarepa, who went into the mountains and stayed there. The long retreat puts that into a calendar. A teaching that has been heard once becomes a teaching that has been lived through every season. Fourth, the people who come out. Some retreatants go on to teach, which is part of how the whispered lineage keeps passing. Others simply return to their families and jobs, and carry it quietly. These retreats are kept in Tibet, India and Nepal, and in Europe and North America too. This week began with the light of the Pure Land, then the diamond vehicle, three vehicles at once, the ancient ones, hidden treasure, the whispered lineage. Today: a door, closed on purpose, for a long time.
screen: `THREE YEARS AND THREE FORTNIGHTS.` · `A DAY OF SESSIONS, BEFORE DAWN.` · `PRACTICE OVER LEARNING ABOUT IT.` · `THE PEOPLE WHO COME OUT.` · then, large: `THREE YEARS, THREE FORTNIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. You don't need three years. You need one small practice, done every day this month. Choose it now: this two-minute sit, a single bow in the morning, one breath before you eat. Something you can keep on your worst day. Say it to yourself once, plainly. Then do it now, for the length of this sit, as the first day of the month. The bell holds the time.
The three-year retreat. A Tibetan retreat of three years and three fortnights, kept by the Kagyu and other schools, with practice from before dawn into the night. Today's word.
Your line: three years, three fortnights. Today, write down the one practice you chose, and mark today as day one. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: In the Kagyu and other Tibetan schools, practitioners enter a closed retreat of three years and three fortnights, following a daily schedule of practice sessions from before dawn into the night under a retreat teacher.

original.note: Tibetan: lo sum chok sum, three years, three fortnights, the name of the retreat.

trapdoor: what you thought: a very long vacation from the world.
what it means: a closed retreat of three years and three fortnights, with practice from before dawn into the night.
what a scholar hears: the Kagyu stress on practice over learning, Naropa's books set down, put into a calendar.

notes: The length 'three years and three fortnights' comes from the index carry and Tibetan tradition; the reasons for the extra fortnights are left unstated on purpose.
'Some retreatants go on to teach' is a general claim; soften to 'some' if a Keeper prefers.
Retreat content (prostrations, mantra, visualization; the practices descended from Naropa in some Kagyu retreats) is described generally; confirm.
Retreats held in Europe and North America as well as Tibet, India and Nepal: confirm. No teachers or dates named on purpose.
Week-end day (1275–1281): the teach closes by looking back over the week.
Tibetan ལོ་གསུམ་ཕྱོགས་གསུམ (lo sum chok sum): confirm spelling and pronunciation guide.
